front: A 100 W bulb and a 2000 J snack: how long could that energy run the bulb?
why: t = E/P estimation with a snack; supporting power/energy arithmetic

front: A 1000 kg car at 20 m/s brakes to rest. Work done by brakes?
why: Work by brakes = change in KE; the standard work-energy calculation

front: A 2 kg mass falls 5 m. Its speed on impact (g = 10) is:
why: v = sqrt(2gh) from energy conservation is calculated on every exam

front: A 60 kg person climbs 3 m of stairs. What distinguishes the work from the power?
why: Work vs power on stairs; restates the same-work-double-power card

front: A ball thrown straight up is at half its maximum height. How is its energy divided?
why: Energy split at half max height and the v0/sqrt(2) trap; common discrete

front: A block oscillating on a spring has {{c1::zero}} kinetic energy at maximum compression.
why: KE zero at max compression, all elastic PE; standard oscillation energy fact

front: A block slides down a frictionless ramp of height $h$ and then compresses a spring. Which relation gives maximum compression?
why: mgh = kx^2/2 for ramp-to-spring; classic energy-conservation setup

front: A box is carried to the second floor by ramp or by stairs. Compare work against gravity and total muscular work.
why: Ramp vs stairs work comparison; conceptual application of path independence

front: A cyclist delivering 100 W of mechanical power at 20 percent efficiency dissipates about {{c1::400 W}} as heat.
why: Efficiency to heat-dissipation arithmetic; second-step application

front: A horizontal total-energy line is drawn across a potential-energy curve. What do the vertical gap and the intersections mean?
why: Reading KE and turning points off a PE curve; passage graph skill

front: A jumper's legs push over distance $d$ to reach height $h$. What relation applies?
why: Push-off work equals PE gained; biomechanics application

front: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of {{c1::energy}}, equal to {{c1::3.6 MJ}}.
why: Kilowatt-hour conversion is units trivia

front: A pendulum released from height $h$ reaches a lowest-point speed equal to the square root of {{c1::$2gh$}}.
why: Pendulum lowest-point speed sqrt(2gh); restates the drop-speed calculation

front: A pole vaulter approaches at 9 m/s. What does the energy budget say about the achievable bar height?
why: Pole-vault height estimate restates v^2/2g conversion; trivia application

front: A pulley system has a mechanical advantage of 4. If you pull the rope 8 m, how far does the load move?
why: Worked pulley distance example; restates the MA distance trade-off card

front: A pulley with mechanical advantage 4 requires the rope to be pulled {{c1::4 times}} the load's rise.
why: MA of 4 means 4x rope pulled; work in = work out for machines

front: A resting adult's basal metabolic power is about {{c1::100 W}}.
why: Basal metabolic rate of 100 W is estimation trivia

front: Climbing stairs twice as fast changes work and power how?
why: Same work, double power when climbing faster; asked essentially every year

front: Does a pulley system reduce the work needed to lift a load?
why: Machines never reduce work, only force; core simple-machine idea

front: Does the work-energy theorem account for heat produced by friction?
why: How friction heat fits into the work-energy theorem; supporting reasoning

front: Doubling a car's speed multiplies its braking distance by {{c1::4}}.
why: Doubling speed quadruples braking distance; yearly proportional-reasoning discrete

front: Efficiency is defined as {{c1::useful energy output divided by total energy input}}.
why: Efficiency = useful output / total input; used in many physics passages

front: Elastic potential energy of a spring equals one half of {{c1::$kx^2$}}.
why: Elastic PE = 1/2 kx^2 is tested every year

front: Estimate the kinetic energy of a 70 kg sprinter at 10 m/s and compare it with one food Calorie.
why: Sprinter KE vs food Calorie is estimation trivia

front: For a mass dropped onto a spring, maximum compression obeys {{c1::$mgh = kx^2/2$}} when $h$ is measured to {{c1::the lowest point}}.
why: Mass dropped onto spring: mgh = kx^2/2 with h to the lowest point; common trap

front: Gravitational potential energy change depends only on {{c1::the vertical displacement}}.
why: Delta PE depends only on vertical displacement; path independence tested every year

front: How can a force change direction of motion without changing speed?
why: Perpendicular force does no work and cannot change speed; common conceptual item

front: How do tendons improve running economy?
why: Tendon elastic energy storage; biomechanics passage context

front: How do you find the work done by a variable force without calculus?
why: Work as area under an F-x graph; standard graph-reading step on every exam

front: How do you get the work done by a gas from a PV diagram?
why: PV-diagram work as area; thermodynamics core that is tested yearly

front: How is the mechanical work done by the left ventricle per beat estimated?
why: Ventricular work as P dV; physiology passage application

front: How is work calculated, and when does a force do zero work?
why: Work formula and zero-work condition; duplicates the cloze W = Fd cos card

front: How much work does a waiter do on a tray carried at constant speed across a level floor?
why: Waiter carrying a tray does zero work; classic discrete

front: How much work does gravity do on a satellite over one circular orbit?
why: Gravity does zero work over a circular orbit; restates the perpendicular-force card

front: Human metabolic efficiency in converting food energy to work is roughly:
why: Human 20-25 percent efficiency; restates the efficiency card's example

front: In an isothermal ideal-gas expansion $\Delta U = 0$, so the heat absorbed equals {{c1::the work done by the gas}}.
why: Isothermal expansion Q = W; thermodynamics content belonging to another deck

front: Is the work done by a spring positive or negative while a mass is pulled away from equilibrium?
why: Sign of spring work while stretching; supporting negative-work reasoning

front: Kinetic energy is {{c1::½mv²}} and gravitational potential energy near Earth is {{c2::mgh}}.
why: KE = 1/2 mv^2 and PE = mgh are the foundation of every energy problem

front: Lowering a dumbbell slowly is an eccentric contraction, in which the muscle does {{c1::negative}} work.
why: Eccentric contraction as negative work; biomechanics application

front: Of $mgh$, $mv$, $kx$, and $Pt$, the expressions carrying joules are {{c1::$mgh$ and $Pt$}}.
why: Dimensional screening of energy expressions; units skill

front: On a force-versus-position graph for a spring, the triangular area under the line equals {{c1::$kx^2/2$}}.
why: Triangle area for spring work restates the F-x area and 1/2 kx^2 cards

front: On a potential-energy curve, a valley is {{c1::stable}} equilibrium while a peak is {{c1::unstable}} equilibrium.
why: Valley stable, peak unstable on a PE curve; common passage reasoning

front: On a potential-energy-versus-position curve, motion accelerates toward {{c1::lower potential energy}} and equilibrium sits where {{c1::the curve is flat}}.
why: Force from PE-curve slope; restates the stable/unstable equilibrium card

front: One food Calorie (1 kcal) equals about {{c1::4184 J}}.
why: kcal to joule conversion is trivia usually supplied if needed

front: Power output climbing a staircase of height $h$ in time $t$ is {{c1::$P = mgh/t$}}.
why: P = mgh/t is the standard MCAT power calculation

front: Spring potential energy is:
why: Near-restatement of the elastic PE cloze card

front: The area under a power-versus-time graph equals {{c1::the total energy delivered}}.
why: Area under a P-t graph is energy; supporting graph skill

front: The work-energy theorem says the net work done on an object equals {{c1::its change in kinetic energy}}.
why: Work-energy theorem W_net = delta KE; tested every year

front: Two frictionless slides drop the same height but differ in shape. Compare the final speeds.
why: Same drop height gives same final speed regardless of path; classic discrete

front: Two objects with equal KE but different mass: the lighter one has:
why: Equal KE, lighter object faster; common comparison

front: What defines a conservative force?
why: Conservative force definition and examples; tested every administration

front: What does negative work by a force tell you physically?
why: Meaning of negative work; common conceptual item

front: What is gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface, and why is the reference height arbitrary?
why: PE = mgh with arbitrary reference level; only changes matter

front: What is power, and what are its two common formulas?
why: Power P = W/t and P = Fv; core formulas used every year

front: What is the formula for kinetic energy, and how does it scale with speed?
why: KE scales with v^2; the quadrupling result is a yearly discrete

front: What is the power dissipated by drag on an object falling at terminal velocity?
why: P = mgv at terminal velocity; classic power application

front: When is $P = Fv$ valid, and what does it explain about cars?
why: Validity of P = Fv and fixed-power car reasoning; restates the power card

front: Which unit measures energy?
why: Joule vs watt vs newton; quick units discrete

front: Why can no potential energy be defined for friction?
why: Why friction has no potential energy; restates the conservative-force card

front: Why does the centripetal force do no work?
why: Centripetal force does no work; restates the perpendicular-force card

front: Why does walking uphill cost more energy than level walking at the same speed?
why: Uphill walking costs more energy; generic restatement of work against gravity

front: With a rough floor between ramp and spring, the energy chain becomes {{c1::$mgh - f_k d = kx^2/2$}}.
why: Energy chain with friction: mgh - f d = kx^2/2; standard multi-step setup

front: With friction present, the change in mechanical energy is {{c1::$-f_k d$}}, where $d$ is path length.
why: Mechanical energy lost to friction = f_k d over path length; used every year

front: Work by a constant force is {{c1::$W = Fd\cos\theta$}}, with $\theta$ between force and displacement.
why: W = Fd cos(theta) is the definition every work problem starts from

front: Work done by a gas expanding at constant pressure is {{c1::$W = P\Delta V$}}.
why: W = P dV for constant-pressure gas work; tested yearly in thermodynamics

front: Work-energy plus friction gives braking distance {{c1::$v^2/(2\mu_k g)$}}, which is independent of {{c1::mass}}.
why: Braking distance v^2/(2 u g) independent of mass; common derivation
